title: Dalpicilib combined with cetuximab in patients with HPV-negative, anti-PD-1-resistant recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: A phase II trial

paper_content.abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is characterised by hyperactivation of the cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) pathway. As immunotherapy has become the first-line treatment for HNSCC, resistance to anti-programmed death-1 (PD-1) agents has emerged as a pivotal challenge. This prospective, single arm, phase II study (NCT05721443) evaluated the efficacy and safety of dalpiciclib, a CDK4/6 inhibitor, combined with cetuximab in patients with anti-PD-1-resistant, HPV-negative recurrent and/or metastatic HNSCC. Patients diagnosed with p16-negative R/M HNSCC resistant to first-line anti-PD-1 therapy without prior cetuximab treatment were enroled. Patients received oral dalpiciclib (150 mg daily on days 1-21 of each 28-day cycle) and intravenous cetuximab (400 mg/m2 on day 1 of cycle 1, followed by 250 mg/m2 weekly in each cycle). The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR), secondary endpoints were overall survival, progression-free survival, duration of response, and safety. Between March 2023 and November 2024, a total of 28 patients were enroled. The ORR was 67.9% (19/28; 95% confidence interval [CI], 49.0%-82.0%), which met our primary endpoint. With a median follow-up of 9.2 months (interquartile range [IQR], 5.98-14.12), the median progression-free survival was 7.0 months (95% CI, 4.13-not reached [NR]), and the median overall survival was 17.0 months (95% CI, 10.75-23.25). Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in all patients, predominantly grade 1-2. Grade 3 TRAEs included neutrophil count decreased (9/28, 32.1%) and white blood cell count decreased (9/28, 32.1%). No grade 4 or 5 TRAEs were observed. Dalpiciclib combined with cetuximab was well-tolerated and showed promising efficacy in patients with anti-PD-1-resistant, HPV-negative recurrent and/or metastatic HNSCC.
paper_content.introduction:
Patients diagnosed with recurrent and/or metastatic (R/M) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) have poor outcomes, with a median overall survival (OS) of 8–10 months1,2. In recent years, immunotherapy has significantly improved clinical outcomes in patients with R/M HNSCC and has increasingly emerged as a first-line treatment for HNSCC. However, pembrolizumab combined with chemotherapy results in an objective response rate (ORR) of 36% and a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 4.9 months, revealing that a considerable number of patients rarely benefit from immunotherapy3.

The incidence of human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative HNSCC is greater than that of HPV-related HNSCC. However, compared with HPV-related HNSCC, HPV-negative HNSCC is often associated with a lower response rate and poorer survival with immunotherapy4,5. HPV-negative HNSCC is characterised by hyperactivation of the cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) pathway, accompanied by CCND1 amplification and CDKN2A deficiency. Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is highly expressed in more than 90% of HNSCC cases and can activate the CDK4/6-cyclin D complex and ultimately drive cancer cell growth by promoting the progression of the cell cycle through the G1 phase, facilitating the malignant transformation of cancer cells6. This provides a rationale for the combination of CDK4/6 and EGFR inhibitors.

Cetuximab, an IgG1 monoclonal antibody against EGFR, binds to the extracellular domain of EGFR and thereby inhibits the tyrosine kinase activity of cancer cells7. Cetuximab is the standard salvage therapy for HNSCC patients refractory to first-line immunotherapy. However, the efficacy of cetuximab monotherapy as a second-line treatment was modest, with an objective response rate of 13% and a median PFS of 2.3 months1. A previous study reported that palbociclib, a selective CDK4/6 inhibitor, resulted in promising outcomes when combined with cetuximab in patients with platinum-resistant or cetuximab-resistant, HPV-negative R/M HNSCC8. However, the anti-tumour activity of the combination of CDK4/6 and EGFR inhibitors is unknown in patients with immunotherapy-resistant, HPV-negative R/M HNSCC.

Here, we report that dalpiciclib, a selective CDK4/6 inhibitor, combined with cetuximab has a promising objective response and considerable toxicity in patients with anti-PD-1-resistant, HPV-negative HNSCC.
paper_content.results:
Between March 2023 and November 2024, a total of 31 patients were screened, and 28 patients were ultimately enrolled in this study (Fig. 1B). Baseline demographics and disease characteristics are presented in Table 1. The median patient age was 58 years (range, 30–75). The primary site of the tumour mainly originated from the oral cavity. The majority of patients (26/28, 92.9%) experienced locoregional recurrence, and only two patients (7.1%) experienced locoregional recurrence with metastases. Fourteen patients (50.0%) had previously received PD-1 inhibitors with chemotherapy, and ten patients (35.7%) had previously received PD-1 inhibitors with vascular epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors in the first-line setting. Tissue specimens were available for 21 (75.0%) patients.

By the data cut-off date on March 3rd, 2025, the median follow-up duration was 9.2 months (IQR 5.98–14.12). Ten patients were still on treatment. The median number of treatment cycles was 4.5 (range, 1–14) for cetuximab and 4.5 (range, 1–14) for dalpiciclib. During the study period, two patients (7.1%) discontinued the study treatment because they could undergo surgery after effective treatment, and one of them achieved a pathological complete response.

In the first stage, among the 14 evaluable participants, 3 patients experienced disease progression, 1 had stable disease, and 9 achieved a PR. In the final analysis, among 28 evaluable patients, 19 achieved a PR, 6 had stable disease, and 3 experienced disease progression. The ORR was 67.9% (95% CI, 49.0%–82.0%; Fig. 2A), which met the primary endpoint. The median DOR was 9.0 months (95% CI, 3.35–14.59; Fig. 2B). A decrease in the sum of the target lesions was observed in 25 patients (89.3%).

At the time of analysis, 16 PFS events occurred. The median PFS was 7.0 months (95% CI, 4.13-NR; Fig. 3A), and the 6-month PFS rate was 53.6%. Ten (32.1%) patients died (9 due to disease progression and one due to haemorrhage). The median OS was 17.0 months (95% CI, 10.75–23.25; Fig. 3B), and the 12-month OS rate was 67.9%.

Baseline tumour tissues from 22 patients were eligible for PD-L1 CPS examination. Among these patients, 19 had a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1, and 6 had a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 20. In populations with a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1, the ORR was 68.4% (95% CI, 45.8%-84.8%), the median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI, 1.52–9.08), and the median OS was 17.0 months (95% CI, 7.21–26.79). In populations with a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 20, the ORR was 66.7% (95% CI, 29.6%–90.7%), the median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI, 1.89–8.71), and the median OS was not reached (Supplementary Fig. 1).

The TRAEs across all cycles are shown in Table 2. TRAEs occurred in all patients, predominantly grades 1–2. The most common TRAEs were decreased neutrophil count (25/28, 89.3%), decreased white blood cell count (25/28, 89.3%), and acneiform rash (16/28, 57.1%). Grade 3 TRAEs occurred in 35.7% (10/28) of the patients, including a decreased neutrophil count (9/28, 32.1%) and a decreased white blood cell count (9/28, 32.1%). The patients rapidly recovered after symptomatic treatment within one week, except for one patient with a grade oral ulcer who recovered after nearly three weeks. No grade 4 or 5 TRAEs were observed.

During the study period, 85.7% (24/28) of the patients received a dose reduction of dalpiciclib, and no patients received a dose reduction of cetuximab. No patients discontinued the treatment because of intolerable toxicity.

Baseline tumour tissues from 20 patients were eligible for next-generation sequencing. The most frequently mutated gene was TP53 (17/20, 85%), followed by TERT (14/20, 70%), TTN (9/20, 45%), FAT1 (6/20, 30%), and CDNK2A (6/20, 30%). The most common gene amplifications were CCND1 (5/20, 25%), FGF4 (5/20, 25%), FGF3 (5/20, 25%), and FGF9 (5/20, 25%; Fig. 4A). Among the 20 patients, 9 had abnormal mutations of CDK4-related genes (4 had CDKN2A deletion, 3 had CCND1 amplification, and 2 had both CDKN2A deletion and CCND1 amplification). The ORR was 81.8% vs. 33.3% (Z = −2.20; P = 0.028), the median PFS was 14.3 vs. 4.3 months (HR 0.26 [95% CI 0.07−0.91]; P = 0.035), and the median OS was not reached vs. 8.5 months (HR 0.23 [95% CI 0.05−1.06]; P = 0.060) in populations without abnormal mutations of CDK4-related genes compared with those with abnormal CDK4-related genes (Supplementary Fig. 2A, B). For the CCND1 amplification analysis, the ORR was 60.0% vs. 60.0% (Z = 0.00, P = 1.000), and the median PFS was 14.3 vs. 3.3 months (HR 0.22 [95% CI 0.01−0.45], P = 0.007), and the median OS was not reached vs. 8.5 months (HR 0.21 [95% CI 0.02−0.75], P = 0.024) in the population without CCND1 amplification compared with the population with CCND1 amplification (Supplementary Fig. 2C, D). With respect to the results of the TP53 mutation analysis, the ORR was 66.7% vs. 58.8% (Z = −0.26, P = 0.798), the median PFS was 14.3 vs. 7.0 months (HR 0.28 [95% CI 0.08−1.11], P = 0.127), and the median OS was not reached vs. 17.7 months (HR unevaluated, P = 0.208), respectively, in the population without TP53 mutation compared with the population with TP53 mutation (Supplementary Fig. 2E, F).

The median TMB was 2.5 per Mb (range, 0.4–8.7), and all patients had microsatellite-stable disease. Substitution of KCNMA1 and TNXB and amplification of TPCN2 were more frequent in nonresponders than in responders (CR+PR; Supplementary Data 1 and 2), while no significant difference in TMB was observed (Fig. 4B). The percentage of lymphocytes significantly increased in responders at the time they achieved the best response compared with baseline (Fig. 4C). However, no significant change in the percentage of lymphocytes was observed in nonresponders (Fig. 4D).

Four patients received subsequent anti-PD-1 therapy after treatment failed with dalpiciclib plus cetuximab. Two patients who responded to dalpiciclib plus cetuximab achieved a PR to subsequent anti-PD-1 rechallenge therapy, whereas the other two patients who did not respond to dalpiciclib plus cetuximab did not respond to subsequent anti-PD-1 therapy (Fig. 4E and Supplementary Fig. 3). For tumour immune microenvironment analysis, we observed that neither baseline CD8+ T cells, Tregs, natural killer (NK) cells nor the CD8+/Treg and CD8+/CD56 ratios were associated with response, PFS or OS in participants receiving dalpiciclib with cetuximab therapy (Supplementary Fig. 4).
paper_content.methods:
The trial protocol was approved by the ethics committee of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital. The trial was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. All the participants signed written informed consent prior to enrolment (the first participant was enroled on March 7th, 2023, and the last participant was enroled on November 1st, 2024). The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05721443, https://register.clinicaltrials.gov/, first posted on February 10th, 2023). In our trial, dalpiciclib and imaging examinations were provided free of charge for all enrolled patients.

This study was an investigator-initiated, single-arm, single-centre phase II trial conducted at Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital. The eligible participants were aged 18–75 years and had histologically confirmed R/M HNSCC; had received at least one cycle of anti-PD-1 therapy in the R/M setting; had at least one measurable lesion according to the Response Evaluation Criteria In Solid Tumours (RECIST) version 1.135; had radiographic confirmation of disease progression or clinical judgement indicating no further benefit from anti-PD-1 therapy; had confirmed HPV-negative disease by immunohistochemistry (IHC); had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1; and had acceptable bone marrow and organ function.

Participants were excluded if they had previously received cetuximab or tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting EGFR; were known to be hypersensitive to recombinant humanised EGFR monoclonal antibodies or CDK4/6 inhibitors; had other types of cancer (excluding cured skin basal cell carcinoma, skin squamous cell carcinoma, carcinoma in situ of the cervix, and early prostate cancer) within 5 years; had received haematopoietic growth factors within one week prior to the study treatment; had active human immunodeficiency virus or treponema pallidum infection; were unable to swallow the drugs; or had abnormal coagulation function.

Participants received cetuximab intravenously at an initial dose of 400 mg/m² followed by a weekly maintenance dose of 250 mg/m2. Dalpiciclib was administered orally at a dose of 150 mg once daily for 21 consecutive days, followed by a 7-day break. Each 28-day period was considered a treatment cycle. Treatment was continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or patient withdrawal, whichever occurred first.

Dalpiciclib treatment was stopped if a grade 2 treatment-related adverse event (TRAE) occurred and was resumed if the TRAE recovered to grade 0 or 1 within 12 weeks. If a patient experienced a grade 3 or higher TRAE, the dose was reduced to 125 mg/day. If the patient was still unable to tolerate this dose, the dose was reduced stepwise to 100 mg/day or to 75 mg/day on the basis of the investigator’s assessment. Dalpiciclib was permanently discontinued if grade 3 or higher TRAEs occurred and failed to recover to grade 0 or 1 within 12 weeks.

Imaging examinations were conducted by computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging at baseline, every two cycles through the first year, and every 3 months thereafter. The response to treatment was determined according to RECIST 1.1, assessed by a specialised radiologist and confirmed by two other masking radiologists. Survival information was obtained from participants every 3 months during follow-up. TRAEs were collected during the treatment period and 1 month (3 months if serious adverse events occurred) after treatment withdrawal and were graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. The detailed study protocol is included in the Supplementary Information file.

The primary endpoint was the ORR, defined as the proportion of patients with a partial response (PR) or complete response (CR) according to RECIST 1.1. Secondary endpoints included OS (defined as the time from enrolment to death from any cause), PFS (defined as the time from enrolment to the first disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first), duration of response (DOR; defined as the interval from the first time that patients achieved a CR or PR to the first disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first), and safety. Exploratory endpoints included the ORR, PFS, and OS in populations with PD-L1 CPSs ≥ 1 and 20 and the ORR, PFS, and OS in individuals with abnormal mutations of CDK4-related genes (CDK4 amplification, CCND1 amplification, or CDKN2A deletion).

Tumour tissue samples (archival paraffin-embedded specimens from the last 2 years or fresh tumour biopsies) and blood samples were collected from the enrolled patients. HPV status was confirmed on the basis of p16 expression detected by IHC (CINtec p16 Histology [Ventana, Tucson, AZ]) using formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples. A targeted sequencing library was generated using a next-generation sequencing panel (YouSuTM, OrigiMed) according to the established standard operating protocol. DNA (50–250 ng) from each sample was used for DNA library preparation as follows: first, DNA was fragmented using the M220 focused ultrasonicator Covaris (Covaris, Woburn, MA, USA) to 150–220 bp; second, the DNA fragments were end-polished A-tailed and ligated with adaptors; then, the exons of 242 cancer-related genes and the introns of 43 genes were captured and amplified by polymerase chain reaction. After quality control and quantification using a LabChip GXII Touch HT (PerkinElmer) and a Qubit 3 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher), the DNA libraries were sequenced on the Illumina-Novaseq 6000 Platform (Illumina Incorporated, San Diego, CA) by paired-end 150-bp sequencing to a mean unique depth of 1000× coverage.

Single-nucleotide variations were identified by MuTect (version 1.7; Broad Institute, Cambridge, MA, USA). Insertion deletions were identified using PINDEL (version 0.2.5). The functional effects of the GAs were annotated using SnpEff 3.0. Copy number variation regions were identified using Control-FREEC (version 9.7; Institute Cochin, Paris, France) with the following parameters: window=50000 and step=10000. Gene fusions were detected using an in-house developed pipeline. Gene rearrangements were assessed using the Integrative Genomics Viewer. The tumour mutation burden (TMB) was estimated by counting the number of coding somatic mutations, including single-nucleotide variations and insertions deletions, per kilobase of sequence examined for each patient. The visual analysis of cancer genomics was performed with the “maftools” and “ggplot2” R packages. Biomarker analysis for tissue samples was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital, and written informed consent to obtain these samples for analysis was obtained from all participants.

Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) were analysed via multiplex immunofluorescence using the following primary antibodies: rabbit anti-human CD4 (Servicebio, cat. no. GB150062; 1:1000), mouse anti-human CD8 (Servicebio, cat. no. GB12068; 1:500), rabbit anti-human CD56 (Servicebio, cat. no. GB112671; 1:500), and rabbit anti-human FOXP3 (Servicebio, cat. no. GB152325; 1:500). Briefly, tissue sections underwent deparaffinization and rehydration, followed by antigen retrieval. The sections were incubated in 3% H₂O₂ in an enclosed humid chamber for 25 min to block endogenous peroxidase activity, after which they were washed on a decolourising shaker. The sections were blocked with 10% goat anti-rabbit serum for 30 min and then incubated with the primary antibody at 4°C overnight. After the cells were washed, an HRP-conjugated secondary antibody was applied for 50 min at room temperature, followed by incubation at room temperature for 10 mins. Antibody stripping preceded repetition of the blocking-primary-secondary-TSA-stripping cycle for the remaining three primary antibodies. Finally, the sections were counterstained with DAPI, quenched with an autofluorescence quencher, mounted with anti-fluorescence quenching medium, and imaged via spectral-based systems with panoramic section scanning.

Historical data revealed that the ORR for second-line treatment with cetuximab monotherapy was 13%. The study adopted a Simon’s two-stage design to minimise the number of subjects exposed to ineffective treatment (Fig. 1A). On the basis of the expected ORR of 33% for dalpiciclib combined with cetuximab, assuming an α of 0.05 (two-sided) and a power of 80%, we aimed to enrol 14 participants in the first stage. If the number of responders (CR+PR) was no more than 1, the study was terminated because of insufficient efficacy. If more than one participant achieved a CR or PR, another 12 participants were recruited in the second stage. A total of 26 participants were enrolled. If the total number of responders (CR+PR) across both stages was more than 6, the combination therapy was considered effective.

Efficacy and safety were analysed in patients who received at least one dose of the study drug. Continuous variables are expressed as medians (ranges), and categorical variables are expressed as frequencies and percentages. The 95% confidence interval (CI) of the ORR was estimated using the Clopper–Pearson method. The median PFS, OS, and DOR were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and their 95% CIs were estimated using the Brookmeyer–Crowley method (IBM SPSS Statistics 27.0). Comparisons of the TMB and gene mutation frequency between responders and nonresponders were performed using the Mann–Whitney test and Fisher’s exact test, respectively. Comparisons of the percentage of lymphocytes during treatment were performed using the paired t test method. A P-value < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The study addresses a significant clinical need and presents encouraging efficacy and safety data for dalpiciclib plus cetuximab in a challenging patient population. While the single-arm design and limited biomarker sample size restrict definitive conclusions, the results are hypothesis-generating and relevant for future research. I recommend revision, with a focus on:
1. Deeper correlative biomarker analyses (linking genomic features to outcomes):
• I recommend the authors perform detailed subgroup analyses to determine if specific genomic alterations—such as TP53 mutation, CCND1 amplification, or their combination—are associated with differential response rates, PFS, or OS. Given the established roles of these alterations in HNSCC biology and therapy resistance, such analyses would provide valuable insight into potential biomarkers of response to dalpiciclib plus cetuximab.
• Additionally, please explore whether patients with CCND1 amplification or other cell cycle pathway alterations had higher response rates to this regimen, as this could support a precision medicine approach for future studies.
2. More detailed reporting and interpretation of immune cell changes:
• The authors should, if possible, provide more granular data on immune cell subsets—such as CD8+ T cells, Tregs, and natural killer (NK) cells—rather than reporting only total lymphocyte percentages. These subsets play distinct and sometimes opposing roles in anti-tumor immunity and are well-established as prognostic and predictive biomarkers in HNSCC.
• Please clarify whether changes in immune infiltration (such as the CD8+/Treg ratio or NK cell abundance) were associated with clinical outcomes in your cohort.
3. Clearer discussion of the limitations and the exploratory nature of biomarker findings:
• The authors should highlight the exploratory nature and potential significance of findings such as KCNMA1, TNXB, and TPCN2 alterations in nonresponders. While these genes may plausibly contribute to resistance mechanisms through known signaling pathways, their roles as biomarkers in HNSCC or in the context of CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy are not established in the current literature.
• Please also discuss limitations such as the small biomarker cohort, lack of functional validation, and the need for independent confirmation.
4. Improved contextualization with existing literature and justification of study design choices:
• The manuscript would benefit from more direct comparison to outcomes with other regimens (e.g., cetuximab monotherapy, other CDK4/6 inhibitors), as well as a rationale for the single-arm design and chosen dosing strategy.
If these revisions are addressed, the manuscript will make a valuable contribution to the field and provide a strong foundation for future research in this area.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper explore Dalpicilib in combination with cetuximab after failure of anti-PD1.
This is a small monoarm study well conducted.
We observe a clear signal of efficacy with high response rate and promising PFS and OS even if it is difficult to be confident in a mOS of 17 months with only 9.2 months of median PFS.
This drug remains toxic with 85% of patinets who need to reduce the dose: in further studies perhaps the schedule/dosage should be modified.
In the discussion the response rate to cetuximab alo,e after anti-PD1 is 20% in the interlink study and this level should probably be indicated. But clearly the combination alpicilib/cetuximab seems better.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
1. Although the protocol stated that the full analysis set (FAS) is to consist of "all enrolled subjects who have taken the study drug at least once", the study's analysis population apparently excludes 2 withdrawals (Figure 1B). Unless they withdrew consent, they should be included in the analyses. They can be used for OS analyses regardless.
2. The statement in the Introduction, "The incidence of human papillomaviruses (HPV)-negative HNSCC is higher than that of HPV-related HNSCC, which is often associated with lower response rate and poorer survival with immunotherapy.", seems reversed.
3. The 95% confidence interval for PFS extends down to 0. This seems unlikely and should be checked.
4. The legend of Fig. 4A) should include descriptions of the two marginal bar charts.
Congratulations on these important results.

## Abstract

Human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is characterised by hyperactivation of the cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) pathway. As immunotherapy has become the first-line treatment for HNSCC, resistance to anti-programmed death-1 (PD-1) agents has emerged as a pivotal challenge. This prospective, single arm, phase II study (NCT05721443) evaluated the efficacy and safety of dalpiciclib, a CDK4/6 inhibitor, combined with cetuximab in patients with anti-PD-1-resistant, HPV-negative recurrent and/or metastatic HNSCC. Patients diagnosed with p16-negative R/M HNSCC resistant to first-line anti-PD-1 therapy without prior cetuximab treatment were enroled. Patients received oral dalpiciclib (150 mg daily on days 1-21 of each 28-day cycle) and intravenous cetuximab (400 mg/m2 on day 1 of cycle 1, followed by 250 mg/m2 weekly in each cycle). The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR), secondary endpoints were overall survival, progression-free survival, duration of response, and safety. Between March 2023 and November 2024, a total of 28 patients were enroled. The ORR was 67.9% (19/28; 95% confidence interval [CI], 49.0%-82.0%), which met our primary endpoint. With a median follow-up of 9.2 months (interquartile range [IQR], 5.98-14.12), the median progression-free survival was 7.0 months (95% CI, 4.13-not reached [NR]), and the median overall survival was 17.0 months (95% CI, 10.75-23.25). Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in all patients, predominantly grade 1-2. Grade 3 TRAEs included neutrophil count decreased (9/28, 32.1%) and white blood cell count decreased (9/28, 32.1%). No grade 4 or 5 TRAEs were observed. Dalpiciclib combined with cetuximab was well-tolerated and showed promising efficacy in patients with anti-PD-1-resistant, HPV-negative recurrent and/or metastatic HNSCC.

---

## Introduction

Patients diagnosed with recurrent and/or metastatic (R/M) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) have poor outcomes, with a median overall survival (OS) of 8–10 months1,2. In recent years, immunotherapy has significantly improved clinical outcomes in patients with R/M HNSCC and has increasingly emerged as a first-line treatment for HNSCC. However, pembrolizumab combined with chemotherapy results in an objective response rate (ORR) of 36% and a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 4.9 months, revealing that a considerable number of patients rarely benefit from immunotherapy3.

The incidence of human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative HNSCC is greater than that of HPV-related HNSCC. However, compared with HPV-related HNSCC, HPV-negative HNSCC is often associated with a lower response rate and poorer survival with immunotherapy4,5. HPV-negative HNSCC is characterised by hyperactivation of the cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) pathway, accompanied by CCND1 amplification and CDKN2A deficiency. Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is highly expressed in more than 90% of HNSCC cases and can activate the CDK4/6-cyclin D complex and ultimately drive cancer cell growth by promoting the progression of the cell cycle through the G1 phase, facilitating the malignant transformation of cancer cells6. This provides a rationale for the combination of CDK4/6 and EGFR inhibitors.

Cetuximab, an IgG1 monoclonal antibody against EGFR, binds to the extracellular domain of EGFR and thereby inhibits the tyrosine kinase activity of cancer cells7. Cetuximab is the standard salvage therapy for HNSCC patients refractory to first-line immunotherapy. However, the efficacy of cetuximab monotherapy as a second-line treatment was modest, with an objective response rate of 13% and a median PFS of 2.3 months1. A previous study reported that palbociclib, a selective CDK4/6 inhibitor, resulted in promising outcomes when combined with cetuximab in patients with platinum-resistant or cetuximab-resistant, HPV-negative R/M HNSCC8. However, the anti-tumour activity of the combination of CDK4/6 and EGFR inhibitors is unknown in patients with immunotherapy-resistant, HPV-negative R/M HNSCC.

Here, we report that dalpiciclib, a selective CDK4/6 inhibitor, combined with cetuximab has a promising objective response and considerable toxicity in patients with anti-PD-1-resistant, HPV-negative HNSCC.

---

## Results

Between March 2023 and November 2024, a total of 31 patients were screened, and 28 patients were ultimately enrolled in this study (Fig. 1B). Baseline demographics and disease characteristics are presented in Table 1. The median patient age was 58 years (range, 30–75). The primary site of the tumour mainly originated from the oral cavity. The majority of patients (26/28, 92.9%) experienced locoregional recurrence, and only two patients (7.1%) experienced locoregional recurrence with metastases. Fourteen patients (50.0%) had previously received PD-1 inhibitors with chemotherapy, and ten patients (35.7%) had previously received PD-1 inhibitors with vascular epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors in the first-line setting. Tissue specimens were available for 21 (75.0%) patients.

By the data cut-off date on March 3rd, 2025, the median follow-up duration was 9.2 months (IQR 5.98–14.12). Ten patients were still on treatment. The median number of treatment cycles was 4.5 (range, 1–14) for cetuximab and 4.5 (range, 1–14) for dalpiciclib. During the study period, two patients (7.1%) discontinued the study treatment because they could undergo surgery after effective treatment, and one of them achieved a pathological complete response.

In the first stage, among the 14 evaluable participants, 3 patients experienced disease progression, 1 had stable disease, and 9 achieved a PR. In the final analysis, among 28 evaluable patients, 19 achieved a PR, 6 had stable disease, and 3 experienced disease progression. The ORR was 67.9% (95% CI, 49.0%–82.0%; Fig. 2A), which met the primary endpoint. The median DOR was 9.0 months (95% CI, 3.35–14.59; Fig. 2B). A decrease in the sum of the target lesions was observed in 25 patients (89.3%).

At the time of analysis, 16 PFS events occurred. The median PFS was 7.0 months (95% CI, 4.13-NR; Fig. 3A), and the 6-month PFS rate was 53.6%. Ten (32.1%) patients died (9 due to disease progression and one due to haemorrhage). The median OS was 17.0 months (95% CI, 10.75–23.25; Fig. 3B), and the 12-month OS rate was 67.9%.

Baseline tumour tissues from 22 patients were eligible for PD-L1 CPS examination. Among these patients, 19 had a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1, and 6 had a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 20. In populations with a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1, the ORR was 68.4% (95% CI, 45.8%-84.8%), the median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI, 1.52–9.08), and the median OS was 17.0 months (95% CI, 7.21–26.79). In populations with a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 20, the ORR was 66.7% (95% CI, 29.6%–90.7%), the median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI, 1.89–8.71), and the median OS was not reached (Supplementary Fig. 1).

The TRAEs across all cycles are shown in Table 2. TRAEs occurred in all patients, predominantly grades 1–2. The most common TRAEs were decreased neutrophil count (25/28, 89.3%), decreased white blood cell count (25/28, 89.3%), and acneiform rash (16/28, 57.1%). Grade 3 TRAEs occurred in 35.7% (10/28) of the patients, including a decreased neutrophil count (9/28, 32.1%) and a decreased white blood cell count (9/28, 32.1%). The patients rapidly recovered after symptomatic treatment within one week, except for one patient with a grade oral ulcer who recovered after nearly three weeks. No grade 4 or 5 TRAEs were observed.

During the study period, 85.7% (24/28) of the patients received a dose reduction of dalpiciclib, and no patients received a dose reduction of cetuximab. No patients discontinued the treatment because of intolerable toxicity.

Baseline tumour tissues from 20 patients were eligible for next-generation sequencing. The most frequently mutated gene was TP53 (17/20, 85%), followed by TERT (14/20, 70%), TTN (9/20, 45%), FAT1 (6/20, 30%), and CDNK2A (6/20, 30%). The most common gene amplifications were CCND1 (5/20, 25%), FGF4 (5/20, 25%), FGF3 (5/20, 25%), and FGF9 (5/20, 25%; Fig. 4A). Among the 20 patients, 9 had abnormal mutations of CDK4-related genes (4 had CDKN2A deletion, 3 had CCND1 amplification, and 2 had both CDKN2A deletion and CCND1 amplification). The ORR was 81.8% vs. 33.3% (Z = −2.20; P = 0.028), the median PFS was 14.3 vs. 4.3 months (HR 0.26 [95% CI 0.07−0.91]; P = 0.035), and the median OS was not reached vs. 8.5 months (HR 0.23 [95% CI 0.05−1.06]; P = 0.060) in populations without abnormal mutations of CDK4-related genes compared with those with abnormal CDK4-related genes (Supplementary Fig. 2A, B). For the CCND1 amplification analysis, the ORR was 60.0% vs. 60.0% (Z = 0.00, P = 1.000), and the median PFS was 14.3 vs. 3.3 months (HR 0.22 [95% CI 0.01−0.45], P = 0.007), and the median OS was not reached vs. 8.5 months (HR 0.21 [95% CI 0.02−0.75], P = 0.024) in the population without CCND1 amplification compared with the population with CCND1 amplification (Supplementary Fig. 2C, D). With respect to the results of the TP53 mutation analysis, the ORR was 66.7% vs. 58.8% (Z = −0.26, P = 0.798), the median PFS was 14.3 vs. 7.0 months (HR 0.28 [95% CI 0.08−1.11], P = 0.127), and the median OS was not reached vs. 17.7 months (HR unevaluated, P = 0.208), respectively, in the population without TP53 mutation compared with the population with TP53 mutation (Supplementary Fig. 2E, F).

The median TMB was 2.5 per Mb (range, 0.4–8.7), and all patients had microsatellite-stable disease. Substitution of KCNMA1 and TNXB and amplification of TPCN2 were more frequent in nonresponders than in responders (CR+PR; Supplementary Data 1 and 2), while no significant difference in TMB was observed (Fig. 4B). The percentage of lymphocytes significantly increased in responders at the time they achieved the best response compared with baseline (Fig. 4C). However, no significant change in the percentage of lymphocytes was observed in nonresponders (Fig. 4D).

Four patients received subsequent anti-PD-1 therapy after treatment failed with dalpiciclib plus cetuximab. Two patients who responded to dalpiciclib plus cetuximab achieved a PR to subsequent anti-PD-1 rechallenge therapy, whereas the other two patients who did not respond to dalpiciclib plus cetuximab did not respond to subsequent anti-PD-1 therapy (Fig. 4E and Supplementary Fig. 3). For tumour immune microenvironment analysis, we observed that neither baseline CD8+ T cells, Tregs, natural killer (NK) cells nor the CD8+/Treg and CD8+/CD56 ratios were associated with response, PFS or OS in participants receiving dalpiciclib with cetuximab therapy (Supplementary Fig. 4).

---

## Methods

The trial protocol was approved by the ethics committee of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital. The trial was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. All the participants signed written informed consent prior to enrolment (the first participant was enroled on March 7th, 2023, and the last participant was enroled on November 1st, 2024). The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05721443, https://register.clinicaltrials.gov/, first posted on February 10th, 2023). In our trial, dalpiciclib and imaging examinations were provided free of charge for all enrolled patients.

This study was an investigator-initiated, single-arm, single-centre phase II trial conducted at Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital. The eligible participants were aged 18–75 years and had histologically confirmed R/M HNSCC; had received at least one cycle of anti-PD-1 therapy in the R/M setting; had at least one measurable lesion according to the Response Evaluation Criteria In Solid Tumours (RECIST) version 1.135; had radiographic confirmation of disease progression or clinical judgement indicating no further benefit from anti-PD-1 therapy; had confirmed HPV-negative disease by immunohistochemistry (IHC); had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1; and had acceptable bone marrow and organ function.

Participants were excluded if they had previously received cetuximab or tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting EGFR; were known to be hypersensitive to recombinant humanised EGFR monoclonal antibodies or CDK4/6 inhibitors; had other types of cancer (excluding cured skin basal cell carcinoma, skin squamous cell carcinoma, carcinoma in situ of the cervix, and early prostate cancer) within 5 years; had received haematopoietic growth factors within one week prior to the study treatment; had active human immunodeficiency virus or treponema pallidum infection; were unable to swallow the drugs; or had abnormal coagulation function.

Participants received cetuximab intravenously at an initial dose of 400 mg/m² followed by a weekly maintenance dose of 250 mg/m2. Dalpiciclib was administered orally at a dose of 150 mg once daily for 21 consecutive days, followed by a 7-day break. Each 28-day period was considered a treatment cycle. Treatment was continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or patient withdrawal, whichever occurred first.

Dalpiciclib treatment was stopped if a grade 2 treatment-related adverse event (TRAE) occurred and was resumed if the TRAE recovered to grade 0 or 1 within 12 weeks. If a patient experienced a grade 3 or higher TRAE, the dose was reduced to 125 mg/day. If the patient was still unable to tolerate this dose, the dose was reduced stepwise to 100 mg/day or to 75 mg/day on the basis of the investigator’s assessment. Dalpiciclib was permanently discontinued if grade 3 or higher TRAEs occurred and failed to recover to grade 0 or 1 within 12 weeks.

Imaging examinations were conducted by computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging at baseline, every two cycles through the first year, and every 3 months thereafter. The response to treatment was determined according to RECIST 1.1, assessed by a specialised radiologist and confirmed by two other masking radiologists. Survival information was obtained from participants every 3 months during follow-up. TRAEs were collected during the treatment period and 1 month (3 months if serious adverse events occurred) after treatment withdrawal and were graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. The detailed study protocol is included in the Supplementary Information file.

The primary endpoint was the ORR, defined as the proportion of patients with a partial response (PR) or complete response (CR) according to RECIST 1.1. Secondary endpoints included OS (defined as the time from enrolment to death from any cause), PFS (defined as the time from enrolment to the first disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first), duration of response (DOR; defined as the interval from the first time that patients achieved a CR or PR to the first disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first), and safety. Exploratory endpoints included the ORR, PFS, and OS in populations with PD-L1 CPSs ≥ 1 and 20 and the ORR, PFS, and OS in individuals with abnormal mutations of CDK4-related genes (CDK4 amplification, CCND1 amplification, or CDKN2A deletion).

Tumour tissue samples (archival paraffin-embedded specimens from the last 2 years or fresh tumour biopsies) and blood samples were collected from the enrolled patients. HPV status was confirmed on the basis of p16 expression detected by IHC (CINtec p16 Histology [Ventana, Tucson, AZ]) using formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples. A targeted sequencing library was generated using a next-generation sequencing panel (YouSuTM, OrigiMed) according to the established standard operating protocol. DNA (50–250 ng) from each sample was used for DNA library preparation as follows: first, DNA was fragmented using the M220 focused ultrasonicator Covaris (Covaris, Woburn, MA, USA) to 150–220 bp; second, the DNA fragments were end-polished A-tailed and ligated with adaptors; then, the exons of 242 cancer-related genes and the introns of 43 genes were captured and amplified by polymerase chain reaction. ## Abstract

Human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is characterised by hyperactivation of the cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) pathway. As immunotherapy has become the first-line treatment for HNSCC, resistance to anti-programmed death-1 (PD-1) agents has emerged as a pivotal challenge. This prospective, single arm, phase II study (NCT05721443) evaluated the efficacy and safety of dalpiciclib, a CDK4/6 inhibitor, combined with cetuximab in patients with anti-PD-1-resistant, HPV-negative recurrent and/or metastatic HNSCC. Patients diagnosed with p16-negative R/M HNSCC resistant to first-line anti-PD-1 therapy without prior cetuximab treatment were enroled. Patients received oral dalpiciclib (150 mg daily on days 1-21 of each 28-day cycle) and intravenous cetuximab (400 mg/m2 on day 1 of cycle 1, followed by 250 mg/m2 weekly in each cycle). The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR), secondary endpoints were overall survival, progression-free survival, duration of response, and safety. Between March 2023 and November 2024, a total of 28 patients were enroled. The ORR was 67.9% (19/28; 95% confidence interval [CI], 49.0%-82.0%), which met our primary endpoint. With a median follow-up of 9.2 months (interquartile range [IQR], 5.98-14.12), the median progression-free survival was 7.0 months (95% CI, 4.13-not reached [NR]), and the median overall survival was 17.0 months (95% CI, 10.75-23.25). Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in all patients, predominantly grade 1-2. Grade 3 TRAEs included neutrophil count decreased (9/28, 32.1%) and white blood cell count decreased (9/28, 32.1%). No grade 4 or 5 TRAEs were observed. Dalpiciclib combined with cetuximab was well-tolerated and showed promising efficacy in patients with anti-PD-1-resistant, HPV-negative recurrent and/or metastatic HNSCC.

## Introduction

Patients diagnosed with recurrent and/or metastatic (R/M) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) have poor outcomes, with a median overall survival (OS) of 8–10 months1,2. In recent years, immunotherapy has significantly improved clinical outcomes in patients with R/M HNSCC and has increasingly emerged as a first-line treatment for HNSCC. However, pembrolizumab combined with chemotherapy results in an objective response rate (ORR) of 36% and a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 4.9 months, revealing that a considerable number of patients rarely benefit from immunotherapy3.

The incidence of human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative HNSCC is greater than that of HPV-related HNSCC. However, compared with HPV-related HNSCC, HPV-negative HNSCC is often associated with a lower response rate and poorer survival with immunotherapy4,5. HPV-negative HNSCC is characterised by hyperactivation of the cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) pathway, accompanied by CCND1 amplification and CDKN2A deficiency. Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is highly expressed in more than 90% of HNSCC cases and can activate the CDK4/6-cyclin D complex and ultimately drive cancer cell growth by promoting the progression of the cell cycle through the G1 phase, facilitating the malignant transformation of cancer cells6. This provides a rationale for the combination of CDK4/6 and EGFR inhibitors.

Cetuximab, an IgG1 monoclonal antibody against EGFR, binds to the extracellular domain of EGFR and thereby inhibits the tyrosine kinase activity of cancer cells7. Cetuximab is the standard salvage therapy for HNSCC patients refractory to first-line immunotherapy. However, the efficacy of cetuximab monotherapy as a second-line treatment was modest, with an objective response rate of 13% and a median PFS of 2.3 months1. A previous study reported that palbociclib, a selective CDK4/6 inhibitor, resulted in promising outcomes when combined with cetuximab in patients with platinum-resistant or cetuximab-resistant, HPV-negative R/M HNSCC8. However, the anti-tumour activity of the combination of CDK4/6 and EGFR inhibitors is unknown in patients with immunotherapy-resistant, HPV-negative R/M HNSCC.

Here, we report that dalpiciclib, a selective CDK4/6 inhibitor, combined with cetuximab has a promising objective response and considerable toxicity in patients with anti-PD-1-resistant, HPV-negative HNSCC.

## Results

Between March 2023 and November 2024, a total of 31 patients were screened, and 28 patients were ultimately enrolled in this study (Fig. 1B). Baseline demographics and disease characteristics are presented in Table 1. The median patient age was 58 years (range, 30–75). The primary site of the tumour mainly originated from the oral cavity. The majority of patients (26/28, 92.9%) experienced locoregional recurrence, and only two patients (7.1%) experienced locoregional recurrence with metastases. Fourteen patients (50.0%) had previously received PD-1 inhibitors with chemotherapy, and ten patients (35.7%) had previously received PD-1 inhibitors with vascular epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors in the first-line setting. Tissue specimens were available for 21 (75.0%) patients.

By the data cut-off date on March 3rd, 2025, the median follow-up duration was 9.2 months (IQR 5.98–14.12). Ten patients were still on treatment. The median number of treatment cycles was 4.5 (range, 1–14) for cetuximab and 4.5 (range, 1–14) for dalpiciclib. During the study period, two patients (7.1%) discontinued the study treatment because they could undergo surgery after effective treatment, and one of them achieved a pathological complete response.

In the first stage, among the 14 evaluable participants, 3 patients experienced disease progression, 1 had stable disease, and 9 achieved a PR. In the final analysis, among 28 evaluable patients, 19 achieved a PR, 6 had stable disease, and 3 experienced disease progression. The ORR was 67.9% (95% CI, 49.0%–82.0%; Fig. 2A), which met the primary endpoint. The median DOR was 9.0 months (95% CI, 3.35–14.59; Fig. 2B). A decrease in the sum of the target lesions was observed in 25 patients (89.3%).

At the time of analysis, 16 PFS events occurred. The median PFS was 7.0 months (95% CI, 4.13-NR; Fig. 3A), and the 6-month PFS rate was 53.6%. Ten (32.1%) patients died (9 due to disease progression and one due to haemorrhage). The median OS was 17.0 months (95% CI, 10.75–23.25; Fig. 3B), and the 12-month OS rate was 67.9%.

Baseline tumour tissues from 22 patients were eligible for PD-L1 CPS examination. Among these patients, 19 had a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1, and 6 had a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 20. In populations with a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1, the ORR was 68.4% (95% CI, 45.8%-84.8%), the median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI, 1.52–9.08), and the median OS was 17.0 months (95% CI, 7.21–26.79). In populations with a PD-L1 CPS ≥ 20, the ORR was 66.7% (95% CI, 29.6%–90.7%), the median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI, 1.89–8.71), and the median OS was not reached (Supplementary Fig. 1).

The TRAEs across all cycles are shown in Table 2. TRAEs occurred in all patients, predominantly grades 1–2. The most common TRAEs were decreased neutrophil count (25/28, 89.3%), decreased white blood cell count (25/28, 89.3%), and acneiform rash (16/28, 57.1%). Grade 3 TRAEs occurred in 35.7% (10/28) of the patients, including a decreased neutrophil count (9/28, 32.1%) and a decreased white blood cell count (9/28, 32.1%). ## Methods

The trial protocol was approved by the ethics committee of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital. The trial was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. All the participants signed written informed consent prior to enrolment (the first participant was enroled on March 7th, 2023, and the last participant was enroled on November 1st, 2024). The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05721443, https://register.clinicaltrials.gov/, first posted on February 10th, 2023). In our trial, dalpiciclib and imaging examinations were provided free of charge for all enrolled patients.

This study was an investigator-initiated, single-arm, single-centre phase II trial conducted at Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital. The eligible participants were aged 18–75 years and had histologically confirmed R/M HNSCC; had received at least one cycle of anti-PD-1 therapy in the R/M setting; had at least one measurable lesion according to the Response Evaluation Criteria In Solid Tumours (RECIST) version 1.135; had radiographic confirmation of disease progression or clinical judgement indicating no further benefit from anti-PD-1 therapy; had confirmed HPV-negative disease by immunohistochemistry (IHC); had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1; and had acceptable bone marrow and organ function.

Participants were excluded if they had previously received cetuximab or tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting EGFR; were known to be hypersensitive to recombinant humanised EGFR monoclonal antibodies or CDK4/6 inhibitors; had other types of cancer (excluding cured skin basal cell carcinoma, skin squamous cell carcinoma, carcinoma in situ of the cervix, and early prostate cancer) within 5 years; had received haematopoietic growth factors within one week prior to the study treatment; had active human immunodeficiency virus or treponema pallidum infection; were unable to swallow the drugs; or had abnormal coagulation function.

Participants received cetuximab intravenously at an initial dose of 400 mg/m² followed by a weekly maintenance dose of 250 mg/m2. Dalpiciclib was administered orally at a dose of 150 mg once daily for 21 consecutive days, followed by a 7-day break. Each 28-day period was considered a treatment cycle. Treatment was continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or patient withdrawal, whichever occurred first.

Dalpiciclib treatment was stopped if a grade 2 treatment-related adverse event (TRAE) occurred and was resumed if the TRAE recovered to grade 0 or 1 within 12 weeks. If a patient experienced a grade 3 or higher TRAE, the dose was reduced to 125 mg/day. If the patient was still unable to tolerate this dose, the dose was reduced stepwise to 100 mg/day or to 75 mg/day on the basis of the investigator’s assessment. Dalpiciclib was permanently discontinued if grade 3 or higher TRAEs occurred and failed to recover to grade 0 or 1 within 12 weeks.

Imaging examinations were conducted by computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging at baseline, every two cycles through the first year, and every 3 months thereafter. The response to treatment was determined according to RECIST 1.1, assessed by a specialised radiologist and confirmed by two other masking radiologists. Survival information was obtained from participants every 3 months during follow-up. TRAEs were collected during the treatment period and 1 month (3 months if serious adverse events occurred) after treatment withdrawal and were graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. The detailed study protocol is included in the Supplementary Information file.

The primary endpoint was the ORR, defined as the proportion of patients with a partial response (PR) or complete response (CR) according to RECIST 1.1. Secondary endpoints included OS (defined as the time from enrolment to death from any cause), PFS (defined as the time from enrolment to the first disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first), duration of response (DOR; defined as the interval from the first time that patients achieved a CR or PR to the first disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first), and safety. Exploratory endpoints included the ORR, PFS, and OS in populations with PD-L1 CPSs ≥ 1 and 20 and the ORR, PFS, and OS in individuals with abnormal mutations of CDK4-related genes (CDK4 amplification, CCND1 amplification, or CDKN2A deletion).

Tumour tissue samples (archival paraffin-embedded specimens from the last 2 years or fresh tumour biopsies) and blood samples were collected from the enrolled patients. HPV status was confirmed on the basis of p16 expression detected by IHC (CINtec p16 Histology [Ventana, Tucson, AZ]) using formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples. A targeted sequencing library was generated using a next-generation sequencing panel (YouSuTM, OrigiMed) according to the established standard operating protocol. DNA (50–250 ng) from each sample was used for DNA library preparation as follows: first, DNA was fragmented using the M220 focused ultrasonicator Covaris (Covaris, Woburn, MA, USA) to 150–220 bp; second, the DNA fragments were end-polished A-tailed and ligated with adaptors; then, the exons of 242 cancer-related genes and the introns of 43 genes were captured and amplified by polymerase chain reaction. After quality control and quantification using a LabChip GXII Touch HT (PerkinElmer) and a Qubit 3 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher), the DNA libraries were sequenced on the Illumina-Novaseq 6000 Platform (Illumina Incorporated, San Diego, CA) by paired-end 150-bp sequencing to a mean unique depth of 1000× coverage.

Single-nucleotide variations were identified by MuTect (version 1.7; Broad Institute, Cambridge, MA, USA). Insertion deletions were identified using PINDEL (version 0.2.5). The functional effects of the GAs were annotated using SnpEff 3.0. Copy number variation regions were identified using Control-FREEC (version 9.7; Institute Cochin, Paris, France) with the following parameters: window=50000 and step=10000. Gene fusions were detected using an in-house developed pipeline. Gene rearrangements were assessed using the Integrative Genomics Viewer. The tumour mutation burden (TMB) was estimated by counting the number of coding somatic mutations, including single-nucleotide variations and insertions deletions, per kilobase of sequence examined for each patient. The visual analysis of cancer genomics was performed with the “maftools” and “ggplot2” R packages. Biomarker analysis for tissue samples was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital, and written informed consent to obtain these samples for analysis was obtained from all participants.

Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) were analysed via multiplex immunofluorescence using the following primary antibodies: rabbit anti-human CD4 (Servicebio, cat. no. GB150062; 1:1000), mouse anti-human CD8 (Servicebio, cat. no. GB12068; 1:500), rabbit anti-human CD56 (Servicebio, cat. no. GB112671; 1:500), and rabbit anti-human FOXP3 (Servicebio, cat. no. GB152325; 1:500). Briefly, tissue sections underwent deparaffinization and rehydration, followed by antigen retrieval. The sections were incubated in 3% H₂O₂ in an enclosed humid chamber for 25 min to block endogenous peroxidase activity, after which they were washed on a decolourising shaker. The sections were blocked with 10% goat anti-rabbit serum for 30 min and then incubated with the primary antibody at 4°C overnight. After the cells were washed, an HRP-conjugated secondary antibody was applied for 50 min at room temperature, followed by incubation at room temperature for 10 mins. Antibody stripping preceded repetition of the blocking-primary-secondary-TSA-stripping cycle for the remaining three primary antibodies. Finally, the sections were counterstained with DAPI, quenched with an autofluorescence quencher, mounted with anti-fluorescence quenching medium, and imaged via spectral-based systems with panoramic section scanning.

Historical data revealed that the ORR for second-line treatment with cetuximab monotherapy was 13%. The study adopted a Simon’s two-stage design to minimise the number of subjects exposed to ineffective treatment (Fig. 1A). On the basis of the expected ORR of 33% for dalpiciclib combined with cetuximab, assuming an α of 0.05 (two-sided) and a power of 80%, we aimed to enrol 14 participants in the first stage. If the number of responders (CR+PR) was no more than 1, the study was terminated because of insufficient efficacy. If more than one participant achieved a CR or PR, another 12 participants were recruited in the second stage. A total of 26 participants were enrolled. If the total number of responders (CR+PR) across both stages was more than 6, the combination therapy was considered effective.

Efficacy and safety were analysed in patients who received at least one dose of the study drug. Continuous variables are expressed as medians (ranges), and categorical variables are expressed as frequencies and percentages. The 95% confidence interval (CI) of the ORR was estimated using the Clopper–Pearson method. The median PFS, OS, and DOR were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and their 95% CIs were estimated using the Brookmeyer–Crowley method (IBM SPSS Statistics 27.0). Comparisons of the TMB and gene mutation frequency between responders and nonresponders were performed using the Mann–Whitney test and Fisher’s exact test, respectively. Comparisons of the percentage of lymphocytes during treatment were performed using the paired t test method. A P-value < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The study addresses a significant clinical need and presents encouraging efficacy and safety data for dalpiciclib plus cetuximab in a challenging patient population. While the single-arm design and limited biomarker sample size restrict definitive conclusions, the results are hypothesis-generating and relevant for future research. I recommend revision, with a focus on:
1. Deeper correlative biomarker analyses (linking genomic features to outcomes):
• I recommend the authors perform detailed subgroup analyses to determine if specific genomic alterations—such as TP53 mutation, CCND1 amplification, or their combination—are associated with differential response rates, PFS, or OS. Given the established roles of these alterations in HNSCC biology and therapy resistance, such analyses would provide valuable insight into potential biomarkers of response to dalpiciclib plus cetuximab.
• Additionally, please explore whether patients with CCND1 amplification or other cell cycle pathway alterations had higher response rates to this regimen, as this could support a precision medicine approach for future studies.
2. More detailed reporting and interpretation of immune cell changes:
• The authors should, if possible, provide more granular data on immune cell subsets—such as CD8+ T cells, Tregs, and natural killer (NK) cells—rather than reporting only total lymphocyte percentages. These subsets play distinct and sometimes opposing roles in anti-tumor immunity and are well-established as prognostic and predictive biomarkers in HNSCC.
• Please clarify whether changes in immune infiltration (such as the CD8+/Treg ratio or NK cell abundance) were associated with clinical outcomes in your cohort.
3. Clearer discussion of the limitations and the exploratory nature of biomarker findings:
• The authors should highlight the exploratory nature and potential significance of findings such as KCNMA1, TNXB, and TPCN2 alterations in nonresponders. While these genes may plausibly contribute to resistance mechanisms through known signaling pathways, their roles as biomarkers in HNSCC or in the context of CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy are not established in the current literature.
• Please also discuss limitations such as the small biomarker cohort, lack of functional validation, and the need for independent confirmation.
4. Improved contextualization with existing literature and justification of study design choices:
• The manuscript would benefit from more direct comparison to outcomes with other regimens (e.g., cetuximab monotherapy, other CDK4/6 inhibitors), as well as a rationale for the single-arm design and chosen dosing strategy.
If these revisions are addressed, the manuscript will make a valuable contribution to the field and provide a strong foundation for future research in this area.

Re: Thank you very much for your carefully review. Epidemiologically, the
incidence of human papillomaviruses (HPV)-negative HNSCC is higher than that
of HPV-related HNSCC.1 Mandal et al. reported in an analysis of TCGA found
that HPV-positive HNSCCs had more significant immune infiltration and had
higher T cell levels infiltrated in HPV positive tissues and associated with a
favorable prognosis,2,3 which suggests patients with HPV-positive status may
obtain more benefit from immune checkpoints blockade. Keynote 012 study was
the first clinical trial to evaluate the relationship between HPV status and immune
checkpoints blockade response. 60 patients with PD-L1+ (> 1%) were treated with
pembrolizumab. ORR was 24% (95% CI, 13-40%) in those patients with HPV
positive, and 16% in HPV negative patients (95% CI, 10-23%, P > 0.05).4 In the
Checkmate 141 subgroup analysis, patients with p16 positive tumors tend to
obtain more benefit from nivolumab than the standard treatment group (median
OS: 9.1 months vs. 4.4 months HR: 0.56; 95% CI: 0.32 to 0.99). On the other hand,
in patients with p16 negative disease, the median OS was 7.5 months in the
nivolumab monotherapy group and 5.8 months in the standard treatment group
(HR: 0.73; 95% CI: 0.42 to 1.25).5 These results indicate that HPV positive
HNSCC is often associated with higher response rate and better survival with
immunotherapy. To avoid ambiguity, we changed our statement from "The
incidence of human papillomaviruses (HPV)-negative HNSCC is higher than that
of HPV-related HNSCC, which is often associated with lower response rate and
poorer survival with immunotherapy." to “The incidence of human
papillomaviruses (HPV)-negative HNSCC is higher than that of HPV-related
HNSCC. However, HPV-negative HNSCC is often associated with lower response
rate and poorer survival with immunotherapy compared with that of HPV-related
HNSCC.”
